title: Title: what you own and how it is proved
summary: Title is your legal ownership of land, and in a registration system it is proved by what the public register says, not by what you believe or what a seller tells you. Learning to read a title document tells you who owns the land, what they own, and what other people can claim against it.
body:
Bottom line. Owning land is not the same as being able to prove you own it. In most of Canada, the proof is the public land register. Read the title document yourself before every deal, because everything you are buying, lending against or building on starts there.

In plain English

Title means the legal right to own land. When people say "who has title?" they mean "who legally owns this?" The proof of title depends on the system used where the land sits.

There are two broad systems. In a deeds system, ownership is proved by a chain of documents, called deeds, going back many years. A lawyer reads the chain to check that each transfer was valid. In a title registration system, the government keeps a register. The register itself states who owns the land and what interests affect it. Alberta uses a title registration system, often called the Torrens system, under the Land Titles Act (Alberta). Other places, including some parts of Guyana, use deeds, registration, or a mix [unverified — confirm independently].

The big idea of a Torrens system is that you can generally rely on the register. If the register says a person owns the land, a buyer who deals honestly with that person is usually protected. Lawyers call this indefeasibility, which means the registered title is very hard to defeat. There are exceptions, so the rule is a strong starting point, not a guarantee [unverified — confirm independently].

The framework

When you read a title document, check these parts in order.

  1. The legal description. This is the official description of the land, using plan, block and lot numbers or survey terms. It is not the street address. Confirm it matches the land you think you are buying.
  2. The registered owner. Check the exact name. A company with a similar name is a different person in law.
  3. The type of estate. An estate in land is the type of ownership. A fee simple is the fullest form of private ownership. A leasehold is a right to use land for a period of time.
  4. How co-owners hold it. Joint tenants each own the whole, and if one dies the others take it automatically. Tenants in common each own a share that passes under their own will. This matters later for estate planning.
  5. The list of registrations. These are interests other people hold: mortgages, caveats, easements, liens and restrictive covenants. A caveat in Alberta is a registered notice that someone claims an interest in the land. Each one is a claim you must understand.
  6. The date and the search. A title is a snapshot. Note the date and time of the search. Anything registered after it is not on your copy.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer agrees to buy a lot for 500,000. The seller says "it is all mine, no debts." The developer orders a title search before signing.

The title shows three things. First, the registered owner is the seller and his spouse, as joint tenants. The seller alone cannot sign the transfer. Second, there is a mortgage for 200,000 in favour of a bank. Third, there is a caveat registered by a neighbour claiming a right of access across the back of the lot.

Each one changes the deal. The spouse must also sign. The mortgage must be paid out from the purchase money at closing and discharged, which means formally removed from the title. The caveat must be investigated. If the neighbour has a real right of access, the buildable area may be smaller, and the price may need to drop.

The seller's statement was an assumption. The title was the fact.

Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate lawyer.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to rely on the street address, the tax assessment or the seller's word instead of the title and its legal description. A municipal tax bill shows who the city sends bills to. It does not prove ownership.

The second mistake is to read only the owner's name and skip the list of registrations. The list is where the risk lives.

How you will use it

Make a title search the first document you order, before you make an offer you cannot withdraw. Read it yourself using the six checks above, then write a one-line note against each registration: what it is, who holds it, and whether it must be removed, accepted or investigated. Bring that page to your lawyer. You will spend the meeting on decisions instead of on reading the document aloud.

Keep the search with the deal file and date it. Before closing, or before you sign a loan, ask for a fresh search. A title can change in a week. A new lien, caveat or judgment registered after your first search is still binding, and only a new search will show it. The habit costs a small fee and protects the largest asset in the deal.
checklist: Order a current title search before committing to a deal.
Match the legal description to the land, not the street address.
Confirm the exact registered owner name and how co-owners hold title.
Note the type of estate: fee simple or leasehold.
List every registration and decide: remove, accept or investigate.
Record the date and time of the search; re-search before closing.

selftest.q: A seller shows you a property tax bill in his name and says he owns the land free and clear. Is that enough? What do you check?
selftest.a: No. A tax bill shows who the municipality bills, not legal ownership. In a title registration system like Alberta's, you check the title: the legal description, the exact registered owner and how co-owners hold, the estate type, and every registered interest such as mortgages, caveats, easements and liens. A real estate lawyer must review it before you commit.

apply: Order or open a title for one property you own or are considering and write one line on each registration listed.
sources: Land Titles Act (Alberta), named as the statute governing the Alberta title registration system; specific sections and the exceptions to indefeasibility are not cited and should be confirmed against the current consolidated statute from the Alberta King's Printer. Statements about Guyana's land systems are tagged [unverified — confirm independently]. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not legal advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate lawyer.

title: The conveyance process: agreement, searches, transfer, registration
summary: Conveyancing is the legal process of moving land from a seller to a buyer, and it runs in a fixed order: a binding agreement, searches and conditions, the closing, and registration. Most problems come from steps done out of order, so knowing the sequence lets you see risk before you sign.
body:
Bottom line. A land purchase is a sequence, not a single moment. The agreement sets the rules, the searches test the facts, the closing exchanges money and documents, and registration makes the buyer the owner on the public record. Do the steps in order and keep your exits open until the facts are proved.

In plain English

Conveyancing means the legal work of transferring land. A conveyance is the transfer itself. In daily speech people say "closing a deal," but the closing is only one step of several.

The process has four stages. First, the buyer and seller sign a purchase agreement, which is the contract for the sale. Second, the buyer checks the land: title, survey, zoning, environment and money. Third, at the closing, the buyer's money goes to the seller and the signed transfer goes to the buyer. Fourth, the transfer is registered at the land titles office, which is when the buyer appears on the register as the owner.

Money and documents usually pass through lawyers' trust accounts. A trust account is a separate bank account a lawyer holds for clients' money. It lets the lawyers exchange everything on agreed terms, so neither side hands over value before the other.

The framework

  1. The agreement. Price, deposit, closing date, what is included, and conditions. A condition is a requirement that must be met, or waived, before the buyer must complete. Common conditions are financing, inspection, title review and zoning. Earlier lessons called these conditions precedent.
  2. Searches and due diligence. Due diligence means the checks a careful buyer makes. A title search shows ownership and registrations. A survey shows boundaries and buildings. In Alberta, a Real Property Report is a common survey document for this purpose [unverified — confirm independently]. Add municipal searches for zoning and permits, and environmental reports for past contamination.
  3. Removing or waiving conditions. When you are satisfied, you give written notice that a condition is met or waived. After that, walking away usually costs you the deposit and may cost damages.
  4. Preparing to close. The lawyers prepare the transfer document, a statement of adjustments, and payout letters for any mortgage. The statement of adjustments splits costs such as property tax between buyer and seller up to the closing date.
  5. The closing. Funds and signed documents are exchanged on trust conditions. A trust condition is a binding promise between lawyers about how a document or money may be used.
  6. Registration. The buyer's lawyer registers the transfer and any new mortgage. A fresh title is then issued in the buyer's name. Check it.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer agrees to buy a site for 1,000,000 with a 50,000 deposit. The agreement has three conditions, each with a 30-day deadline: financing, title review and an environmental report.

On day 20 the title review is clean, so his lawyer gives notice that the title condition is satisfied. On day 25 the lender approves 700,000. On day 28 the environmental report finds a buried fuel tank from an old service station. Removing it is estimated at 80,000.

Because the environmental condition is still open, he has a choice. He can walk away and get his deposit back. He can negotiate a price reduction of 80,000. Or he can ask the seller to remove the tank before closing. He negotiates a 70,000 reduction and then waives the condition in writing.

Had he waived all conditions on day 1 to make his offer look stronger, he would have owned an 80,000 problem with no leverage.

Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate lawyer; environmental consultant; land surveyor.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to remove conditions early or sign an offer with no conditions, because a seller or agent says it will win the deal. Conditions are your exits. Each one you remove before the facts are in is an exit you lose.

The second mistake is to assume the deal is finished at the closing. Until the transfer is registered and you have checked the new title, the job is not done.

How you will use it

Keep a one-page conveyancing timeline for every purchase. List each condition, its deadline, who is responsible for the check, and what the result was. Set a reminder several days before each deadline, not on the day. Before you waive any condition, ask your lawyer one question in writing: "What do I lose if I waive this today?"

Use the same timeline when you are the seller. A buyer's conditions are the buyer's exits, and every open condition is a reason the deal may not close. Ask for short deadlines, and track the dates for the buyer's notices. If a deadline passes without a written waiver, the agreement usually tells you what happens next. Read that clause before the date arrives, not after it.
checklist: Read the agreement for price, deposit, closing date and every condition.
Write each condition's deadline and owner on a timeline.
Order title, survey, municipal and environmental searches early.
Waive a condition only in writing and only after the facts are in.
Review the statement of adjustments before closing.
Check the new title after registration.

selftest.q: An agent tells you to submit an offer with no conditions because three other buyers are interested. What do you give up, and how could you protect yourself?
selftest.a: You give up every exit: financing, title, inspection and environmental checks. If a problem appears, you must close anyway or lose your deposit and possibly pay damages. You could do key checks before offering, keep at least a short title and financing condition, or adjust the price to reflect the risk. Ask your real estate lawyer what each waiver costs before deciding.

apply: Make a timeline table for your next purchase with columns for condition, deadline, who checks it, and result.
sources: Process lesson. The Real Property Report is described as a common Alberta survey document and tagged [unverified — confirm independently]. No statute section, rate or fee is cited; conveyancing practice varies by province and by lawyer. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not legal advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate lawyer; environmental consultant; land surveyor.

title: Encumbrances: mortgages, liens, easements, lender consents
summary: An encumbrance is anyone else's right over your land, such as a mortgage, a lien, an easement or a covenant. Some can be paid off, some stay with the land for ever, and some need another person's consent before you can deal with the land.
body:
Bottom line. Owning land does not mean nobody else has rights in it. Every encumbrance limits what you can do, what a lender will lend, or what a buyer will pay. Sort each one into three groups: remove, live with, or get consent.

In plain English

An encumbrance is a right or claim that someone other than the owner holds over the land. It is a burden on the title. Most appear on the title search as registrations, which is why the last lesson told you to read that list carefully.

An encumbrance is not always bad. A utility easement may be the reason the site has power. A covenant may protect the value of every lot in a subdivision. The point is to know what each one does, so the price, the design and the loan all reflect it.

Some encumbrances secure money. A mortgage is a loan secured on land: if the borrower does not pay, the lender can force a sale. A lien is a claim to be paid that is attached to the land. A builder's lien, sometimes called a construction lien, lets a contractor or supplier who was not paid register a claim against the land they improved.

Some encumbrances give use rights. An easement lets someone else use part of your land for a purpose, such as a neighbour's driveway or a utility line. A utility right of way is a common kind. A restrictive covenant is a promise attached to land that limits how it can be used, for example a limit on building height.

And some encumbrances are about permission. A lender's mortgage usually says you cannot sell, transfer or further mortgage the land without its consent.

The framework

  1. List every registration. Take them from the title, in order. The order often matters, because earlier-registered interests usually rank ahead of later ones [unverified — confirm independently].
  2. Classify each one. Money claim, use right, use limit, or consent requirement.
  3. Decide the treatment. Money claims are usually paid out and discharged at closing. Use rights and use limits usually stay with the land and bind future owners. Consent requirements must be satisfied before you act.
  4. Measure the effect on value and design. An easement through the middle of a site can remove buildable area. A covenant can cap density.
  5. Check the documents behind the registration. The title shows only that an interest exists. The registered document says what it actually allows.
  6. Watch for interests that are not on the title. Some claims arise without registration, such as certain unpaid taxes or rights under a statute. Ask your lawyer what searches cover these.

In Alberta, the law on construction liens was revised and the statute renamed the Prompt Payment and Construction Lien Act [unverified — confirm independently]. Deadlines for registering a lien are short and strictly applied [unverified — confirm independently]. Do not rely on any day count without checking the current statute.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer wants to refinance a finished building worth 3,000,000. The title shows four registrations: an existing first mortgage of 1,500,000, a builder's lien of 60,000 from a drywall subcontractor, a utility right of way along the north edge, and a restrictive covenant from the original subdivision limiting the use to residential.

The new lender will lend 1,950,000, but only as a first mortgage on a clean title. The old mortgage must be paid out and discharged. The lien must be resolved: the developer checks the contract, finds the subcontractor was underpaid by 40,000 after a dispute, pays 40,000 into court or settles, and has the lien removed. The right of way stays; the lender accepts it because no building sits on it. The covenant stays too; it matches the actual use.

Without clearing the lien, the refinance would not have closed.

Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate lawyer; construction lawyer for the lien.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to assume that every registration can be paid off. Easements and covenants usually cannot be removed just by paying money. Removing them often needs the other party's agreement or a court order [unverified — confirm independently].

The second mistake is to forget the lender's consent clause. Moving the property into a new company, adding a second mortgage, or leasing a large part of it can all breach the mortgage if the lender did not agree in writing.

How you will use it

For every property, keep an encumbrance table: registration, holder, type, treatment, and effect on value. Update it before any sale, refinance or transfer. When a lender sends a commitment letter, compare its required title conditions with your table on the day it arrives. Pay contractors on time and keep proof, because an unpaid invoice can become a registered claim against the asset that secures all your other financing.
checklist: List every registration on the title in order.
Classify each: money claim, use right, use limit, or consent requirement.
Read the registered document behind each entry, not just the title line.
Decide which to discharge, which to accept, and which need consent.
Check the mortgage for consent clauses before any transfer or new loan.
Ask which claims can exist without appearing on the title.
Pay contractors on time and keep proof of payment.

selftest.q: You plan to move a property into a new company and add a second loan. The title shows a first mortgage, a utility right of way and a restrictive covenant. What must you check first?
selftest.a: Check the first mortgage for consent clauses, because a transfer to a new company and a second mortgage both usually need the lender's written consent. Confirm the right of way and covenant will bind the new owner and do not affect the second lender's terms. A real estate lawyer must review the documents before the transfer.

apply: Build an encumbrance table for one property, with one row per registration and a treatment for each.
sources: Prompt Payment and Construction Lien Act (Alberta) named and tagged [unverified — confirm independently]; lien deadlines, priority rules, and rules for removing easements and covenants are deliberately not stated as numbers or sections and are tagged [unverified — confirm independently]. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not legal advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: real estate lawyer; construction lawyer for liens.

title: Transferring land into a company: triggers, costs, timing
summary: Moving land you own personally into a company is a sale in the eyes of the law and of the tax system, even when you own the company. Before you do it, check the tax trigger and any rollover, transfer fees and sales tax, the lender's consent, spousal consent and the timing.
body:
Bottom line. Moving land into your own company is a real transfer with real consequences. It can trigger tax, fees, sales tax and a lender default, and it can need your spouse's consent. Plan every trigger before the documents are signed, because most of them cannot be undone afterwards.

In plain English

Many developers buy land personally and later want it in a company. The company may offer limited liability, separate the project from the family's other assets, or make financing easier.

The key idea is that a company is a separate person in law, as an earlier lesson explained. So when you transfer land to your company, you are selling it to someone else, even if you own every share. The tax system usually treats it as a disposition, which means a sale, at fair market value. Fair market value is the price a willing buyer and seller would agree on at arm's length, which means between unrelated parties.

That can create a large taxable gain with no cash coming in. In Canada, section 85 of the Income Tax Act (Canada) lets a person transfer certain property to a taxable Canadian corporation and choose a transfer price, within limits, so that the gain is deferred. This is called a rollover. It requires a joint election filed with the Canada Revenue Agency, and some property and some situations do not qualify, such as land held as inventory in some cases [unverified — confirm independently].

The framework

Check each trigger before you sign.

  1. Income tax. Is the transfer a disposition at fair market value? Is a section 85 rollover available? What consideration, meaning payment, will the company give you, such as shares or a promissory note?
  2. Sales tax. Goods and Services Tax (GST) can apply to some sales of real property, especially new or commercial property, and elections and exceptions exist [unverified — confirm independently].
  3. Transfer fees. Some provinces charge a land transfer tax. Alberta is generally understood to charge registration fees rather than a land transfer tax [unverified — confirm independently]. Confirm the current fee schedule.
  4. The lender. Most mortgages need the lender's written consent before the land is transferred. Without it, the transfer can be a default.
  5. Spousal consent. In Alberta, the Dower Act protects a married person's interest in the homestead, meaning the home the couple live in, and generally needs the spouse's written consent to dispose of it [unverified — confirm independently].
  6. Other consents and documents. Leases, insurance, permits, title insurance and municipal records may all need to change.
  7. Timing. The earlier land goes into the company, the less growth is caught in the transfer. Moving it after value has risen means more tax to defer or pay.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer bought a lot personally for 400,000. It is now worth 700,000. He wants it in a new project company. There is a 250,000 mortgage on it.

A straight transfer at 700,000 would be a disposition at fair market value, creating a gain of 300,000 with no cash received. His accountant reviews whether a section 85 rollover is available and, if so, proposes an elected amount of 400,000, the original cost, deferring the gain. The company issues shares to him as consideration and assumes the mortgage.

Then the other triggers. The lender must consent to the company taking over the mortgage, and asks for his personal guarantee. The GST position is reviewed because the company will develop and sell. Registration fees are budgeted. The lot is not his home, so spousal consent is checked and confirmed not to be needed.

Had he transferred the lot when he bought it, there would have been no gain to manage at all.

Professional Sign-Off Required: chartered professional accountant (CPA) and tax lawyer; real estate lawyer.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to register a transfer to the company first and ask the accountant afterwards. A section 85 rollover needs the election and the right consideration, and a lender default cannot be undone by paperwork later.

The second mistake is to transfer land for no stated price, or "for one dollar," thinking it avoids tax. The tax system generally uses fair market value between related parties, whatever the document says [unverified — confirm independently].

How you will use it

Decide early which entity should own each new site, ideally before you buy it. When a transfer is unavoidable, build a trigger list with the seven headings above and get each one answered in writing before any document is signed. Ask your accountant and lawyer to meet together on the plan, since the tax steps and the legal steps depend on each other.

Keep the transfer file permanently. It should hold the valuation, the election, the share issue documents, the lender's consent and the registered transfer. Years later, when the company sells the land or you plan your estate, someone will need to prove the cost, the date and the elected amount. A complete file makes that a short task instead of an expensive reconstruction.
checklist: Decide which entity should own land before buying it.
Treat a transfer to your company as a sale at fair market value.
Ask a CPA whether a section 85 rollover is available and what election is needed.
Check GST and transfer or registration fees.
Get the lender's written consent before transferring mortgaged land.
Check whether spousal consent is needed for a home.
Have the accountant and lawyer agree the plan before anything is signed.

selftest.q: You want to move a rental property you own personally into your holding company. Its value has doubled since you bought it, and it has a mortgage. List the triggers you need answered before signing.
selftest.a: Income tax: a transfer to the company is a disposition at fair market value, so check whether a section 85 rollover is available and what consideration and election are needed. Sales tax: whether GST applies. Fees: registration or transfer costs. Lender: written consent, or the transfer may be a default. Spousal consent: only if it is a home. Other: leases, insurance and title. A CPA, tax lawyer and real estate lawyer must sign off.

apply: Write the seven-trigger list for one property you might move into a company and mark each item as known, unknown or not applicable.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada), section 85 (transfer of property to a corporation), cited by name; confirm current text and eligibility, including for inventory, with a CPA. Dower Act (Alberta) named and its effect tagged [unverified — confirm independently]. GST under the Excise Tax Act (Canada), Alberta registration fees and the absence of a land transfer tax are tagged [unverified — confirm independently]; no rates or fees are stated. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not tax or legal advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: chartered professional accountant (CPA) and tax lawyer; real estate lawyer.
